Backyard Gold Refineries

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Exposed: private plots being rented out to gold smugglers

Unique Selling Point:
Carte Blanche has been invited to film a SAPS raid on a plot in Walkerville, where private landowners have rented out a portion of their plot for an illegal gold refinery.
Possibility of interviewing land owners.


Summary:
Since the the raids on Zama Zamas have intensified, syndicates have moved their gold refining operations off-site. All across the south Rand - from Lenasia to Heidelberg - is a massive network of backyard gold refineries operating quietly on private property. The Kingpins are Zimbabwean, the workers are Malawian and Mozambican.
Syndicates approach private landowners and make them an offer they can't refuse. They will settle all outstanding municipal accounts, pay a monthly rental, and pay a percentage of the profits.
A small refinery is set up on the plot, complete with all equipment and staff.
Then the gold-bearing soil starts arriving. Bags of soil, dug up by Zama Zamas and transported by car, by Bakkie, by taxi, by lorry, even by tipper truck to the plot. Some of the soil is stolen from legitimate mines. Between 200 and 300 tonnes of soil is processed each month.
But now the ground is contaminated by sodium cyanide that is seeping into the ground water in the area.

Further information:
The Hawks have managed to close down two operations, but another 13 are under observation. the source of some of the soil has been traced back to an illegal mining operation in Johannesburg municipality.

Extra Budget Items:
Depending on what is revealed during the raid, we may require another day/half-day of filming.

Script:


BACKYARD GOLD – FINAL

Masa link: It’s early morning here in Walkerville and it’s all systems go. The chopper has just arrived, behind me are heavily armed men who are all ready for this raid.

V/O: A new kind of criminal has entered this neighbourhood. This is not a gold mining area, but as the screws tighten on illegal mining, the syndicates are on the move - and surprisingly – they’re moving in next door.


V/O: Just 10 minutes south of Johannesburg you’ll find this small-scale farming community. It’s a slice of the countryside, with wholesome names like Fruit Farms and Apple Orchards. But something is rotten here, a scourge that threatens every living thing.

Dario: The little dog that stays here died just suddenly. And then after that we also found dead birds and dead chickens.

V/O: The plots are 10 acres, but when a mining syndicate moves in, even 10 acres isn’t big enough.

Rudy: People get the wrong impression. When they say mining people think of digging down into the ground. I mean this thing was totally new. When it happens in your own backyard, it’s actually quite scary, I must say.

V/O: Zama zamas have invaded the ground beneath our feet, but what happens to the soil they dig up? Where do they refine it? A police crackdown is forcing them out of the West Rand, into an unexpected corner of Gauteng.

Masa link: This is Walkerville Fruit Farms. It’s quiet here with a rural atmosphere. But behind these walls, something shady is going down. It’s the last place you’d expect to find organized crime.

V/O: Rudy le Roux has lived here for 33 years. In February two men came to his gate asking to rent his cottage.

Rudy: I said look the place is available but there’s no water or electricity there. So, they said that’s not a problem. So, I said well, what do you do? So, they said no, they’re looking to start a small business.

Masa: And how much rent were they proposing to pay?

Rudy: R3000 a month.

Masa: And you thought you were getting upstanding people?

Rudy: Yes. You know, they were very nice people, they really were. They both were from Zimbabwe as well, they’re from Chipinga area, so me being a Zimbabwean as well…so I said yeah, no problem.

V/O: But within a week, the relationship soured. When the Neighbourhood Watch chased a robbery suspect through Rudy’s property, they discovered an illegal gold refinery.
10:11:52
Rudy: It was this huge flipping thing with sand inside, they had pipes there, there was a big tank at the bottom, you know. And I didn’t even know what it was. I didn’t have a clue. He said no, this is a zama zama operation.

V/O: The police arrested two Mozambicans who were working the operation, but the Zimbabwean bosses remained at large.

Rudy: He then phoned, and he said they’re very sorry for what’s happened here, you know. He says but look, they went to court, they were fined, and they were deported. And when can they come back? So, I said no, no, no, you don’t come back here.

Masa: When can they come back?

Rudy: Yes.

V/O: The makeshift refinery is still in Rudy’s backyard - two portable swimming pools holding tonnes of gold-bearing sand. This was filled with a mixture of water and cyanide that leaches the gold from the gravel, and then stores it in carbon. A network of PVC pipes, now vandalised, leads to a water tank buried in the ground.

Rudy: It’s probably about twenty to thirty thousand rand a day they can make out of that.

Masa: Hmm, it’s a lot of money.

Rudy: Wow!

V/O: What the Zimbabweans really wanted to recover was this valuable gold-bearing sand. But where did it come from?

James: We’ve got a good suspicion. I mean there are a lot of old residual dumps as you know if you drive out in that direction.

V/O: James Wellsted is Executive Vice-President of Investor Relations for Sibanye Stillwater. Their mines are clustered around Randfontein.

James: There are older mines that have been closed, and in fact we’ve got our Cooke operations on care and maintenance. We’re waiting for a closure certificate so we can close them fully. But in the interim that allows illegal miners to gain access to the workings, because we’re not actively working in those areas.

V/O: In Randfontein we found the source of the sand that is being transported to the Midvaal smallholdings. These holes were closed by Sibanye Stillwater, but some have been opened again.

Masa link: So, this is it. This is where the sand comes from on the West Rand. The zamas are just digging holes in the ground to gain access to the old workings of the mine, and the gold-bearing material in the pillars that were left behind.

V/O: But under increased scrutiny on the West Rand, the syndicates are now taking their plunder sixty kilometres south, to be refined in the safety and seclusion of private properties in Midvaal.

Dario: It was trucks and bakkies that would come in and out, and mainly at night. I think trying to avoid being detected by police and residents.

V/O: Dario is a tenant on a Walkerville smallholding. He’s hiding his face because he informed police about illegal activity in a workshop he shared with other tenants.

Dario: When I went in, I would get a headache immediately because of the fumes that would be in the factory. You actually battled to breathe. You couldn't stay. You had to get out of the way.

V/O: This is the next stage in the process. Here are the bags of carbon; the lethal fumes came from this steel boiler used to extract the gold. The criminality is endangering lives, because not only are the chemicals poisonous, but they could also blow up at any second.

Masa: When they did conduct that raid, what did they find on the property?

Dario: Oh, they found acid and carbon and cyanide.

V/O The sodium cyanide is allegedly smuggled over the border from Zimbabwe.
We traced the manufacturers Hebai Chengxin to this factory in China.

In 2015 the port of Tianjin was rocked by a series of deadly blasts, when 700 tonnes of their sodium cyanide exploded in a warehouse.

Sfx: Oh my God!

Mandarin: 2nd blast from far away

V/O: 173 people were killed – most of them firefighters unaware of the deadly fumes. It took 5 days to extinguish the fires and left behind a wasteland.

V/O: This is the same chemical being used in people’s backyards. Not only is the process incredibly dangerous, but could be poisoning the environment, posing a significant health hazard to residents and their animals.

James: They are using things like mercury, cyanide, sulfuric acid as part of the leaching and then refining process, and they’re not following best practice in terms of using the lined dams etc. So, you can get these chemicals which are highly toxic leaking into the water system you know, into the groundwater.

V/O: It’s this threat of contamination that’s most concerning to Midvaal’s Mayor, Peter Teixeira.

Masa: What reassurance can you give to residents in Midvaal that the water is clean?

Mayor: Look, it’s a serious health hazard. So, we do our part, which is test the water, and we advise accordingly. And thus far we’ve not had any problems.

V/O: Midvaal has budgeted over R7 million to help community policing forums combat illegal mining.

Teixeira: We’ve also given our CPFs your thermal drones and they can see exactly what is happening.

V/O: The drones have uncovered twenty-four backyard operations in Midvaal, and ten have already been shut down.

V/O: Law enforcement officials are determined to act.

Steven: So, this is our target area, there’s the mining operation. We’ll do a penetration here through the main gate.

Masa: Okay.

Steven: All the members will surround the property, secure it, so that we don’t get any runners because that’s where the operation’s taking place.

V/O: Community policing, private security and the Hawks are getting ready to swoop on another backyard operation.

Sfx: Chopper, doors slamming, sirens

V/O: Anxious about the highly toxic and explosive chemicals in the area, they’re drawing a line in the sand and going in.

Sfx: These are cable ties, but they act as handcuffs

V/O: The zama zamas could be armed, so they’re taking no chances. A convoy of trucks waits nearby to seize the gold-bearing sand.

Steven: Look there, they’re working there. There’s one guy there on the wall there.

Driver: Okay, tell them there’s guys there, watch them.

Steven: There’s guys on the back wall. Ja

V/O: Within moments, a suspect is arrested.

Gresham: I need cuffs this side, cuffs!

V/O: They’ve been caught by surprise, with little chance of escape.

V/O: By the end of the raid seven suspects are in custody, including the landowner and his son. And this is just one of several refineries in the area.

Sfx: Open!

V/O: Among the suspects are four Mozambicans and one South African, each earning R200 a day from a boss they say is Zimbabwean.

Masa link: I just can’t believe it, it’s just all so brazen. I mean, this is somebody’s back yard!

There’s a sink over there – and there is where all the dangerous chemicals are also thrown into the mix, such as sodium cyanide, and we’ve been warned by the police as well not to get too close to it, because it is so harmful just to even breathe it in.

V/O: But the landlord claimed ignorance, believing this was all just building sand.

Cop: How much were they paying you?

Owner: R3500.

Steven: The owner is well aware of what’s happening here and is complicit in the mining operation.

V/O Midvaal Peace Officer Steven van der Walt is satisfied with the operation.

Steven: There’s been several arrests and as you can see, we’ve estimated approximately two to three hundred tonnes of soil being recovered here.

V/O: These backyard processes can only extract 60% of the gold, so this leftover soil is worth about R780 000. And if that’s what the dregs are worth, then how much are the kingpins making? (pause)

These criminal activities are a danger to life and limb, but will increased law enforcement be able to end the scourge, or is it already too late?

All across the south Rand - from Lenasia to Heidelberg - is a massive network of backyard gold refineries operating quietly on private property. The Kingpins are Zimbabwean, the workers are Malawian and Mozambican. Syndicates approach private landowners and make them an offer they can't refuse. They will settle all outstanding municipal accounts, pay a monthly rental, and pay a percentage of the profits. A small refinery is set up on the plot, complete with all equipment and staff. Then the gold-bearing soil starts arriving. Bags of soil, dug up by Zama Zamas and transported by car, by Bakkie, by taxi, by lorry, even by tipper truck to the plot. Some of the soil is stolen from legitimate mines. Between 200 and 300 tonnes of soil is processed each month. But now the ground is contaminated by sodium cyanide that is seeping into the ground water in the area.
metadata.Further information: The Hawks have managed to close down two operations, but another 13 are under observation. the source of some of the soil has been traced back to an illegal mining operation in Johannesburg municipality.
